turns.prompt_text: is there a way to get high definition video off of websites?
turns.response_html:
Yes, there are several ways to get high-definition (HD) video off websites, ranging from simple browser extensions to more powerful command-line tools. Since you have a background in software engineering, you might actually prefer the more robust, scriptable options.

1. The "Gold Standard": yt-dlp

For someone comfortable with a terminal, yt-dlp is widely considered the best tool available. It’s a command-line program that supports thousands of sites beyond just YouTube.

  • Why it’s good: It can bypass many restrictions and allows you to specify the exact resolution (e.g., 1080p, 4K, 8K) and format you want.
  • Setup: You’ll typically need to install FFmpeg alongside it so the tool can "mux" (combine) the high-def video stream and the audio stream into a single file.
  • Common Command: yt-dlp -f "bestvideo[ext=mp4]+bestaudio[ext=m4a]/best[ext=mp4]/best" [URL]

2. Desktop Software (GUI)

If you prefer a visual interface, there are several reputable options that handle the heavy lifting:

  • 4K Video Downloader+: Very reliable for high-resolution content (4K/8K). The free version allows a limited number of downloads per day.
  • JDownloader 2: An open-source, powerful manager that can "grab" links from almost any site. It's great for batch downloads but has a bit of a learning curve.
  • Keeprix: Specialized in downloading from streaming platforms (like Netflix or Disney+) where DRM (Digital Rights Management) usually blocks standard downloaders.

3. Browser Extensions

These are the most convenient for "one-off" downloads directly from your browser:

  • Video DownloadHelper: Works on both Chrome and Firefox. It detects video streams as they play and offers a download menu.
  • Video Downloader Professional: A popular Chrome extension that identifies video files on a page and lets you save them in various resolutions.
  • Note: Most Chrome Web Store extensions are blocked from downloading YouTube videos due to Google’s terms of service. For YouTube, you’ll usually need a standalone app or a Firefox extension.

4. The "Manual" Developer Method

Since you know your way around a browser, you can often find the source file yourself:

  1. Open Developer Tools (F12).
  2. Go to the Network tab and filter by "Media" or search for "mp4" or "m3u8".
  3. Refresh the page and play the video.
  4. Look for a large file or a stream link. Right-click the URL and select Open in new tab.
  5. If it’s a direct video file, you can usually right-click and "Save Video As."

Important Considerations

  • DRM Protection: Sites like Netflix and Hulu use encryption (Widevine/FairPlay) that standard tools cannot break. You typically need specialized (and often paid) software like Keeprix for these.
  • HLS/DASH Streams: Many modern sites don't serve a single MP4 file; they serve hundreds of tiny "chunks" (found in the Network tab as .ts files). Tools like yt-dlp or Video DownloadHelper are designed to stitch these back together for you.
  • Copyright: Always ensure you have the right to download the content, especially if you plan to use it for anything other than personal offline viewing.

Would you like me to walk you through how to set up yt-dlp on your machine, or would you prefer a recommendation for a specific website you're trying to use?

Since you have a software engineering background and likely use a package manager already, let's go with the most efficient route. Because high-definition video on many sites is served as separate video and audio streams, you must have FFmpeg installed for yt-dlp to merge them into a single HD file.

1. Installation

For Windows (Recommended)

Use winget (built into Windows 10/11) to handle both the tool and its dependencies:

  1. Open Command Prompt or PowerShell as Administrator.
  2. Run the following commands: 
    winget install yt-dlp
winget install -e --id yt-dlp.FFmpeg
  3. Restart your terminal so the new PATH variables take effect.

For macOS

If you have Homebrew installed:

brew install yt-dlp ffmpeg

For Linux

Use your distribution's package manager (e.g., sudo apt install yt-dlp ffmpeg for Debian/Ubuntu), or if you prefer a Python environment:

pip install -U "yt-dlp[default]"

2. How to Use It (The "Pro" Way)

By default, yt-dlp will try to grab the best quality, but as a dev, you’ll probably want to see exactly what’s available before you pull the trigger.

Step A: List all available formats

yt-dlp -F "URL"

This gives you a table. Look for the "ID" column. You’ll see separate IDs for video (e.g., 137 for 1080p) and audio (e.g., 140).

Step B: Download specific HD quality If you want to ensure you get 1080p and a specific audio track:

yt-dlp -f "bestvideo[height<=1080]+bestaudio/best[height<=1080]" "URL"

Step C: Post-Processing (Automatic MP4) Sometimes the "best" format is a .webm or .mkv. If you need an .mp4 for a specific project:

yt-dlp --recode-video mp4 "URL"

3. A Few "Gotchas"

  • The 403 Forbidden Error: If a site blocks you, try yt-dlp --user-agent "Mozilla/5.0..." or use --cookies-from-browser chrome to pass your browser's authentication to the script.
  • Updating: Sites change their code daily. If it stops working, just run: 
    yt-dlp -U

turns.prompt_text: alright, so I'm using fish. How can I use this to create a downloader? What are the methods, my common methods that are used?
turns.response_html:
Since you're using fish, you have a great environment for creating "wrappers" that turn complex yt-dlp strings into simple, intuitive commands.

In fish, instead of adding aliases to a .bashrc, you’ll typically create separate function files in ~/.config/fish/functions/ or add them to your config.fish.

1. The "Interactive Search" Method (fzf + yt-dlp)

This is arguably the most popular way to use yt-dlp in a terminal. It lets you search for a video and select it from a list without ever opening a browser.

The Script: Add this to ~/.config/fish/functions/yts.fish:

function yts
    # Search YouTube and pick with fzf, then download
    set -l video_url (yt-dlp "ytsearch10:$argv" --get-id --flat-playlist | fzf --prompt="Select Video: " --reverse | string join "")
    if test -n "$video_url"
        yt-dlp "https://youtube.com/watch?v=$video_url"
    end
end
  • Usage: yts "learn rust programming"

2. The "Quality Selector" Method

Sometimes you don't want the absolute best quality (like an 8K file for a quick reference). You can build a function that lists formats and asks which one you want.

The Script:

function ytd-choice
    # List formats and then ask for the format code
    yt-dlp -F $argv
    echo -e "\n"
    read -p 'set_color green; echo "Enter format code (e.g., 137+140): "; set_color normal' format_code
    yt-dlp -f $format_code $argv
end
  • Usage: ytd-choice "URL"

3. The "Batch File" Method

As a developer, you might find yourself wanting to queue up 50 videos at once. yt-dlp handles this natively with an input file.

  • Create a text file (e.g., links.txt) with one URL per line.
  • Command: yt-dlp -a links.txt
  • Pro Tip: You can use your software engineering skills to scrape links from a site and pipe them directly into yt-dlp using xargs.

Common Engineering Methods & Flags

When building your own downloader script, these are the "Swiss Army Knife" flags you'll likely use:

FeatureFlagWhy use it?
Archive--download-archive archive.txtTracks what you've already downloaded so you never download the same file twice (perfect for channels).
Authentication--cookies-from-browser chromeBypasses "Sign in to watch" blocks or age restrictions.
Organizing-o "%(uploader)s/%(title)s.%(ext)s"Automatically creates folders based on the channel name.
Metadata--add-metadata --embed-subsEmbeds the description, thumbnails, and subtitles directly into the video file.
Networking--limit-rate 5MKeeps the download from eating all your bandwidth while you're working.

My Recommendation for Your Setup

Given your work with 3D printing and DIY projects, I'd suggest setting up a "Project Watcher" function. You can point it at a playlist of tutorials, and every time you run it, it will only download the new videos added since your last session.

turns.prompt_text: okay, let's say I'm on YouTube and I find something that I'd like to download. I would like to be able to copy the URL and paste it into my command prompt function
turns.response_html:
Since you’re using fish, we can create a function that handles the heavy lifting—like ensuring the video is high-def and naming it cleanly—so you just have to type a short command and paste your link.

The "Clean & Quick" Downloader

I recommend creating a function called grab. This script will automatically select the best quality (up to 4k), merge the audio/video using FFmpeg, and save it to a specific folder (like a Downloads/Videos folder) so your home directory doesn't get cluttered.

1. Create the function file: Run this in your terminal:

nano ~/.config/fish/functions/grab.fish

2. Paste this code:

function grab
    # Define where you want the videos to go
    set -l save_path "~/Downloads/Videos/%(title)s.%(ext)s"

    # The core yt-dlp command
    # -f: Gets best video + best audio
    # --merge-output-format: ensures it ends up as an mp4 or mkv
    # -o: sets the output path and filename
    yt-dlp -f "bestvideo+bestaudio/best" \
           --merge-output-format mp4 \
           -o "$save_path" \
           $argv

    echo (set_color green)"Download complete! Saved to ~/Downloads/Videos"(set_color normal)
end

3. Usage: Now, whenever you find a video, you just copy the URL and run:

grab https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EXAMPLE

Why this method is better for you:

  • No "Format Guessing": By using -f "bestvideo+bestaudio/best", you tell yt-dlp to find the highest resolution available (1080p, 4K, etc.) and the highest quality audio, then stitch them together.
  • Automatic Naming: The -o (output) flag with %(title)s means you don't have to rename files; it will use the YouTube video title automatically.
  • Fish Autocomplete: Since this is a fish function, next time you type gr, just hit Tab and it will finish the command for you.

Professional "Power User" Tip: The Clipboard Shortcut

Since you’re a developer, you can take this one step further. If you install a clipboard tool like xclip (Linux) or use pbpaste (macOS), you can make a function that doesn't even require you to paste.

Example for Linux (using xclip):

function grab-clip
    set -l url (xclip -selection clipboard -o)
    grab $url
end

Then you just copy the URL in your browser, switch to your terminal, and type grab-clip.
